story.title: Apple introduces M6 and M5 Ultra

draft:
Apple’s new M6 and M5 Ultra chips aren’t just a speed bump—they’re a redefinition of on‑device AI compute.

The M6 adds a dedicated neural engine that doubles matrix‑multiply throughput while keeping power draw under the previous generation. For me, that means training small models or running inference locally will finally be a first‑class experience on a Mac, not a cloud‑only luxury. The M5 Ultra pushes the envelope further with 64‑core GPU blocks and unified memory up to 1 TB, essentially turning a laptop into a single‑node AI workstation.

From a software perspective, these silicon upgrades force us to rethink where we place the compute budget. I expect to see more developers offloading transformer inference to the client, which could reshape data‑privacy models and reduce latency for real‑time apps. The challenge will be mastering the new toolchains and profiling the neural engine’s performance quirks before the hype settles.

Will the industry’s shift toward on‑device AI accelerate as Apple’s hardware makes it practical, or will cloud providers still dominate the heavy‑lifting?
